title: Analyze app telemetry with logs and metrics

questions.q: Which KQL operator selects specific columns for the output?

options.why: render draws a chart.
where filters rows.
Correct. project picks, renames or computes columns.
summarize aggregates rows into groups.

questions.hint: One operator chooses which columns appear in the output.
questions.explain: Filter with where, shape with project.

questions.q: You open Logs from a Log Analytics workspace rather than from the Application Insights resource. Which table holds incoming requests?

options.why: requests is the name in Application Insights scope.
That's a custom log table naming pattern, not this table.
That's a different diagnostics table.
Correct. Workspace scope uses AppRequests, AppExceptions, AppDependencies.

questions.hint: Workspace-based tables have App-prefixed names.
questions.explain: Query scope decides table and column names.

questions.q: Which function groups timestamps into fixed hourly intervals for trend analysis?

options.why: Correct. bin rounds each timestamp down into 1-hour buckets.
dcount estimates distinct values.
ago(1h) is a point in time used for filtering.
percentile calculates a latency percentile.

questions.hint: One function rounds timestamps down into fixed-size buckets.
questions.explain: Without bin(), each unique timestamp would form its own group.

questions.q: You want the 20 slowest failed requests from the last hour, sorted by duration. Which operator should end the query?

options.why: take returns an arbitrary 20 rows, not the slowest.
project selects columns; it doesn't limit rows.
Correct. top returns the first N rows sorted by a column.
That groups by duration rather than listing requests.

questions.hint: One operator sorts and limits in a single step.
questions.explain: take for a quick look; top for the highest or lowest values.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A query searches a large traces table for the word timeout in the message column.

rows.text: The has operator uses the term index and is usually faster than contains.
rows.why: has uses term indexing; contains doesn't.

rows.text: dcount() returns an exact distinct count in every case.
rows.why: dcount() estimates; count_distinct() is exact but heavier.

rows.text: Adding render timechart needs a datetime column in the results.
rows.why: timechart requires a datetime column and numeric columns.

rows.text: The take operator returns rows sorted by the column you name.
rows.why: take returns arbitrary rows; top sorts.

questions.hint: Think about term-indexed search, approximate distinct counts, charts needing time, and whether take sorts.
questions.explain: Pick fast operators and remember sampling when counting.

questions.q: Each option starts with `requests | where timestamp > ago(24h)`. Which one gives request count and average duration per hour for each service?

options.text: … | project timestamp, duration, cloud_RoleName | render timechart
options.why: render doesn't aggregate data.

options.text: … | summarize count(), avg(duration) by bin(timestamp, 1h), cloud_RoleName
options.why: Correct. bin buckets the time and the by clause groups per service.

options.text: … | take 24 | summarize count(), avg(duration) by cloud_RoleName
options.why: take 24 returns 24 arbitrary rows, not 24 hours.

options.text: … | summarize count(), avg(duration) by timestamp, cloud_RoleName
options.why: Grouping by raw timestamp creates one group per unique time.

questions.hint: Count and average per hour and per service: group by both the time bucket and the role name.
questions.explain: summarize … by bin(timestamp, 1h), cloud_RoleName is the standard trend pattern.

questions.q: Your code tracks a custom event, "document classified", each time the classifier finishes. In which Application Insights table do these rows appear?

options.why: customMetrics holds numeric measurements such as queue depth.
requests holds incoming HTTP requests.
Correct. customEvents stores custom business events that developers track explicitly.
traces holds application log messages.

questions.hint: Business events you track yourself have their own table, separate from logs and numbers.
questions.explain: Application Insights tables: requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces (logs), customEvents (business events), customMetrics (numeric measures) and performanceCounters (system metrics).

questions.q: Sampling is enabled in Application Insights. Which aggregation gives an accurate exception total?

options.why: Correct. Each sampled record represents itemCount real events.
count() returns only the number of sampled records.
dcount counts distinct exception types.
An average doesn't give a total.

questions.hint: With sampling, each row may stand for several items. Add up the weights.
questions.explain: Use sum(itemCount) whenever sampling may be active.

questions.q: A failed dependency call to a model inference endpoint shows resultCode 429. What does it indicate?

options.why: Correct. 429 means the endpoint is rate limiting; adjust throughput or retry policies.
Timeouts often have no result code.
That's typically a 500.
KQL query errors don't produce dependency result codes.

questions.hint: 429 is the HTTP code for too many requests.
questions.explain: 429 = throttled, 500 = server failure, no code = timeout or network.

questions.q: After joining exceptions with requests, you see columns named cloud_RoleName and cloud_RoleName1. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Ignore it; the suffix disappears after render
options.why: The suffix is part of the result columns.

options.text: Drop the join and query each table separately
options.why: You'd lose the correlation.
union stacks rows; it doesn't correlate them.

options.text: Rename the columns inside the subquery before the join
options.why: Correct. Renaming first gives unambiguous names in the final project.

questions.hint: A join adds a 1 to duplicate column names. Fix it before joining.
questions.explain: KQL adds a numeric suffix to duplicate column names after a join.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A dependency has an average duration of 200 ms.

rows.text: This proves that nearly all calls finish in about 200 ms.
rows.why: Averages can hide slow tails; check percentiles.

rows.text: Checking the 95th and 99th percentiles can reveal slow outliers.
The Performance view's duration distribution can show a bimodal pattern.
rows.why: It reveals mostly-fast with a slow subset.

questions.hint: An average hides the spread. Look at percentiles and the distribution.
questions.explain: Use percentiles(duration, 50, 95, 99) for latency analysis.

questions.q: An investigator wants the top response codes and exception types for a failing operation, then to open a sample request's full timeline. Where should they start?

options.why: Dashboard tiles summarize; they aren't the drill-down tool.
Performance shows durations, not failure breakdowns.
Correct. It shows top codes, exceptions and failed dependencies, with drill-down to samples.
Live Metrics is real-time, not a failure breakdown.

questions.hint: The Investigate area has a view built for failures, with drill-down to samples.
questions.explain: Built-in views first, then KQL for deeper questions.

questions.q: A classifier catches an exception, logs it and returns a fallback label. Will the exception appear in the Application Insights exceptions table?

options.text: No, only unhandled exceptions are stored
options.why: Handled exceptions can be recorded too.

options.text: Yes, but only in the dependencies table
options.why: Dependencies are outgoing calls, not exceptions.

options.text: No, exceptions go to the traces table with the logs
options.why: traces holds log messages. Exceptions have their own table.

options.text: Yes, if it's recorded; handled ones appear too
options.why: Correct. The exceptions table records both handled and unhandled exceptions with stack traces.

questions.hint: The exceptions table isn't only for crashes.
questions.explain: The exceptions table records errors with stack traces and severity, and both handled and unhandled exceptions appear there when they're recorded.

questions.q: A metrics chart should reveal rare worst-case latency spikes that averages hide. Which aggregation fits?

options.why: Count gives a number of samples, not latency.
Average shows typical behavior and smooths spikes.
Sum totals events over a period.
Correct. Max shows worst-case values.

questions.hint: Rare spikes disappear in an average. Which aggregation keeps the worst value?
questions.explain: Average for typical latency, sum for totals, max for spikes.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team publishes an operations dashboard with tiles from Application Insights.

rows.text: The tiles show live, real-time data at every moment.
rows.why: Tiles refresh on a schedule; use Live Metrics for real time.

rows.text: A teammate with dashboard access but no access to Application Insights sees access errors on those tiles.
rows.why: Viewers need read access to data sources too.

rows.text: Learn suggests keeping a dashboard to about 5–10 tiles.

questions.hint: Dashboard tiles refresh periodically, follow the viewer's own access, and work best in small numbers.
questions.explain: Dashboards are for at-a-glance health; scope access to data as well.

questions.q: A latency tile shows p50 flat at 300 ms while p95 climbs from 1 s to 4 s over a week. What does this indicate?

options.text: All requests are getting four times slower
options.why: p50 is flat, so typical requests aren't slower.
Sampling doesn't selectively drop slow requests.

options.text: Most stay fast; a growing subset degrades
options.why: Correct. A widening p50–p95 gap points to a slow subset, such as one document type.

options.text: The dashboard's refresh schedule is broken
options.why: The trend is consistent, not a refresh glitch.

questions.hint: The median is steady while the tail grows. What does that say about most requests?
questions.explain: Watch percentile gaps, not just averages.

questions.q: New team members open the operations dashboard and don't know what the application does or where the runbooks are. Which best practice addresses this?

options.text: Merge the business and pipeline dashboards into one
options.why: Learn suggests separating concerns into different dashboards.

options.text: Add more tiles so that every metric is visible
options.why: Learn suggests 5–10 focused tiles; more tiles add clutter.

options.text: Name tiles Query 1, Query 2 and so on to keep them short
options.why: Descriptive tile titles are the recommendation.

options.text: Add a Markdown tile at the top with context, runbook links and on-call contacts
options.why: Correct. A Markdown tile gives viewers the context they need.

questions.hint: One tile type is just text.
questions.explain: Dashboard best practices: separate concerns, keep 5–10 tiles, use descriptive tile titles, and include a Markdown tile with context, runbook links and on-call information.

questions.q: During an incident, an engineer wants to pick a service and time range and have all charts update together. Which tool fits?

options.why: Smart detection raises anomaly alerts.
Correct. Parameters such as {TimeRange} and {ServiceName} drive every dependent query.
Dashboard tiles are relatively static.

options.text: An action group for the team
options.why: Action groups send notifications.

questions.hint: Interactive charts that all respond to the same choices need a tool with parameters.
questions.explain: Dashboards for at-a-glance health; workbooks for interactive investigation.

questions.q: A workbook dropdown {ServiceName} allows multi-select. How should a query filter on it?

options.why: == compares to one value.
project selects columns.
Correct. Multi-select becomes a comma-separated list for the in operator.
has is a term search, not a list match.

questions.hint: Multi-select values need a filter that accepts a list.
questions.explain: Multi-select parameters compare several services side by side.

questions.q: A workbook shows a summary grid of services with error counts. Clicking a service should filter the rest of the workbook to that service. What should you configure?

options.text: A second dashboard for each service
options.why: Separate dashboards don't drill down from a click.

options.text: A resource picker parameter at the top
options.why: A resource picker chooses resources, not a service from a grid row.

options.text: A grid link that exports a parameter
options.why: Correct. The exported parameter filters the remaining steps.

options.text: A log search alert for each service
options.why: Alerts notify; they don't filter views.

questions.hint: Clicking a grid row should set something the rest of the workbook reads.
questions.explain: Combine linked grids with conditional visibility for drill-down.

questions.q: Which Azure Monitor alert severity is the most urgent?

options.why: 3 is for notable events without urgency.
4 is verbose diagnostic detail.
1 is Error, one step lower.
Correct. 0 is Critical, for production-impacting failures.

questions.hint: Severities run from 0 to 4. Lower numbers are more urgent.
questions.explain: Severity runs from 0 (Critical) to 4 (Verbose).

questions.q: You need an alert when the 95th-percentile response time of any service exceeds 3 seconds, computed with KQL. Which alert type fits?

options.why: Correct. Log search alerts run KQL queries, including percentiles per service.
Smart detection learns baselines; it doesn't enforce your 3-second SLA.
Tiles don't notify anyone.

options.text: A metric alert on CPU percentage
options.why: CPU isn't response-time percentile per service.

questions.hint: The condition is computed with a KQL query.
questions.explain: Log search alerts give the flexibility AI apps usually need.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A log search alert runs `requests | where success == false | summarize failedCount = count() by cloud_RoleName | where failedCount > 10` every 5 minutes over a 5-minute window, firing when rows > 0.

rows.text: Each returned row identifies a service with more than 10 failures in the window.
rows.why: Rows represent services over the threshold.

rows.text: One alert rule can reference up to ten action groups.
rows.why: The limit is five action groups per rule.

rows.text: Requiring several violations before firing reduces noise from single spikes.
rows.why: You can configure the number of violations.

rows.text: Smart detection makes this manual rule unnecessary.
rows.why: Manual rules enforce known thresholds; smart detection finds novel anomalies.

questions.hint: Each result row can be its own alert. Several violations reduce noise.
questions.explain: Manual log alerts plus smart detection give the widest coverage.

questions.q: When a critical alert fires, the team wants a ticket created in an external system automatically. Which action group action fits?

options.why: SMS notifies a person; it doesn't create tickets.
Severity classifies urgency; it isn't an action.
Push notifies devices only.
Correct. Logic Apps can create a ticket in an external system.

questions.hint: Creating a ticket elsewhere calls for a workflow automation service.
questions.explain: Automated actions: Function, Logic App, webhook, Automation Runbook, Event Hub.

questions.q: A dependency has slowed gradually over three weeks, and no fixed threshold has fired. Which feature is designed to catch this?

options.why: A tile shows data but doesn't alert.
Correct. Smart detection compares against historical norms and spots gradual degradation.
Parameters filter views; they don't alert.

options.text: A metric alert with a static threshold
options.why: Static thresholds miss values that never cross the line.

questions.hint: A slow drift doesn't cross a fixed line. A feature that learns normal behavior can catch it.
questions.explain: Smart detection learns a baseline and alerts on deviations.

questions.q: Five alert rules for the RAG pipeline should all page the same on-call engineer and post to the same team channel. What's the most maintainable setup?

options.text: Copy the same notifications into each rule's condition
options.why: Conditions decide when an alert fires. Notifications belong in action groups.

options.text: One action group with both notifications, referenced by all five rules
options.why: Correct. Action groups are reusable across alert rules.

options.text: Raise every rule to Sev 0 so that notifications go out automatically
options.why: Severity labels urgency. It doesn't send notifications by itself.

options.text: Five action groups, one per rule, each with the same settings
options.why: That duplicates configuration that one reusable action group can hold.

questions.hint: Alert rules have a scope, a condition, a severity, and something reusable that decides who hears about it.
questions.explain: An alert rule has a scope, a condition, an action group and a severity (0 Critical to 4 Verbose). Action groups hold notifications and automated actions, and they're reusable across rules.
